t: Maximum Number That Sum of the Prices Is Less Than or Equal to K — Binary Search with Bit Counting
o: The price of num counts set bits at positions x, 2x, 3x, .... The accumulated price is monotone nondecreasing in num, so we can binary search the largest num whose accumulated price ≤ k. The core subroutine counts, for a fixed bit position p, how many integers in [1, num] have that bit set — a classic O(1) formula using full blocks of length 2^(p+1). Since k ≤ 1e15 and x ≥ 1, the answer fits below 2^58.
k: Accumulated price is monotone in num → binary search the answer.
Count of integers ≤ num with bit p set = ⌊(num+1)/2^(p+1)⌋·2^p + max(0, (num+1) mod 2^(p+1) − 2^p); sum this over p = x, 2x, ....

a.n: Approach 1: Binary search + per-position population count
a.i: Define acc(num) by summing the closed-form bit-count over positions p = x, 2x, ... ≤ num. Binary search the largest num with acc(num) ≤ k over [1, 2^58].
s: Implement count(num, p) with the block formula.
Implement acc(num) looping p from x upward while 2^p ≤ num.
Binary search for the largest cheap num.
a.t: O(log^2(answer)) — about 58 binary-search steps, each summing ≤ 58/x bit-position counts in O(1)

w: Alternative: digit DP over the binary representation computing the accumulated price directly (also O(log^2)); binary search is simpler to get right. Pitfalls: shifting by amounts near 63 in 64-bit languages (guard with the loop condition), and off-by-one in the partial-block term — verify against the k=9,x=1 and k=7,x=2 examples. Follow-up: compute the accumulated price of a range [l, r], or the smallest number with accumulated price exactly k.
